docs.title: A Simple Guide To using Clusters
docs.text: This is a simple guide to get started with using the clusters. it is by no means a exaustive documentation and thereore should not be used as that. as we are ased at wsl this will mostly be tailored to the use of the Hyperion HPC, but the knowledge you are acquiing is transferrable to other HPCs that use the SLURM job scheduler.

docs.title: Step 0: Gain Access to the Cluster
docs.text: To gain access, send an email to IT support.

docs.title: Step 1: Connect to the Cluster
docs.text:
You will need to connect using SSH.

WindowsMac/Linux

The native Windows SSH client cannot connect to the cluster because it is out of date. You will need to install the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), a Windows feature that lets you run a Linux environment directly on your PC. Find installation instructions here.

Open PowerShell and start WSL:

wsl

No additional setup is required. Continue with the steps below.

Connect to Hyperion using SSH:

ssh <username>@hyperion.wsl.ch

Enter your password to connect. You should see a message like this:

Last login: Tue Oct  6 09:08:52 2026 from 10.27.2.186
-----------------------------------------------------------------

  This is Hyperion - the master node of the new WSL Linux cluster.

  Here you can manage your files, compile code and submit
  batch jobs to the queueing system SLURM.

  Please DO NOT run long processes on *this* computer.
  Use the queueing system SLURM instead.

  For information about how to use the cluster, see

    http://hyperion.wsl.ch/

  For technical support please use helpdesk address

    http://intra.wsl.ch/it/helpdesk/Stoerungsmeldung_Cluster1_DE

-----------------------------------------------------------------
[elkhoury@hyperion ~]$

docs.title: Set Up Your Workspace
docs.text:
At this point, it is a good idea to familiarize yourself with basic Linux commands, if you are not already familiar with them. This will make it easier to navigate the cluster's file system. This section provides some basic Unix commands.

If this is your first time using the cluster, create a personal folder on the /storage/ drive to keep your projects separate from those of other users: 

cd /storage              # Go to the storage directory
mkdir <your-username>    # Create a folder
cd <your-username>       # Move into your new folder

docs.title: Prepare Your Development Environment
docs.text:
The software stack on the cluster is not regularly updated, so the latest releases of Python, R, and other tools may not be available. This can be a problem if you need a library that only works with a more recent release.

To use the latest versions of R or Python, install an environment manager such as Conda or Mamba.

Check whether Mamba is installed: 

mamba -h

If you see the following output, Mamba is not installed:

bash: mamba: command not found...

To install it, follow the Installing Mamba guide.

Then test the installation: 

mamba -h

You are now ready to create an environment. Follow the instructions in Using Mamba.

Note: A new copy of R and its packages is installed in each environment. This can create a large number of files and slow down the cluster. It is therefore a good idea to create one environment with the latest version of R and use it for most projects. If a project requires an older version of R, create a separate environment for it.

docs.text:
The easiest way to transfer files is to use a file transfer client such as WinSCP (Windows only) or Cyberduck (Windows and macOS).

docs.title: Running Code
docs.text: You cannot run code directly on the cluster after transferring it. If you do, it will run on the login node, which is slower and less powerful than the compute nodes. To run code on the compute nodes, you must write a job script.

docs.title: The Job Script
docs.text:
A job script tells the scheduler how many resources your job requires, how long it should run, where to send notifications if it succeeds, fails, or is cancelled, what software to use, and what code to run.

A basic job script looks like this:

#!/bin/bash
# Example requesting more resources than the default

#SBATCH --mail-user=charbel.elkhoury@wsl.ch # Your email address
#SBATCH --mail-type=SUBMIT,END,FAIL # Notify you of these events
#SBATCH -o out # Standard output
#SBATCH -e err # Standard error output
#SBATCH --mem=4000M # Request 4 GB of RAM
#SBATCH --time=10:00 # Run for 10 minutes
#SBATCH -n 1 # One core

/storage/elkhoury/mamba/installation/etc/profile.d/mamba.sh
mamba activate r_env_demo
Rscript main.R

Store this file in the same folder as the code you want to run. For example, name it jobscript.sh.

docs.title: Submit a Job Script
docs.text:
Submit the job with the following command:

sbatch jobscript.sh

docs.title: Monitoring a job
docs.text:
After submitting a job with sbatch, you can check whether it is still queued or running with:

squeue -u <username>

Typical output looks like:

JOBID   PARTITION   NAME       USER   ST   TIME     NODES
12345   normal      analysis   ck     R    03:21    1

The most useful columns are:

  • JOBID — unique job identifier
  • NAME — job name
  • ST — job state
  • TIME — how long the job has been running

Common job states include:

State Meaning R Running PD Pending CG Completing

To continuously monitor your jobs, use watch:

watch squeue -u <username>

This refreshes the output every two seconds.

Press Ctrl+C to stop watch.

docs.title: Checking job output and errors
docs.text:
Slurm writes the program's normal output and error messages to files. If your submission script defines them as:

#SBATCH --output=out
#SBATCH --error=err

you will get two files:

out
err

docs.title: Read the output
docs.text:
For a short file:

cat out

For a longer file:

less out

Use the arrow keys to navigate and press q to exit.

To see only the last lines:

tail out

docs.title: Monitor output while the job is running
docs.text:
tail -f out

This displays new output as it is written.

Press Ctrl+C to stop following the file.

You can do the same with the error file:

tail -f err

docs.title: Check for errors
docs.text:
Read the complete error file:

cat err

or inspect it with:

less err

An empty err file generally means that nothing was written to standard error.

Messages in err do not necessarily mean that the job failed. Programs may also write warnings and diagnostic information to standard error.

docs.title: Installing WSL on Windows
docs.text:
WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) allows you to run a Linux environment directly inside Windows.

Requirements: Windows 11 or Windows 10 version 2004 (Build 19041) or newer.

docs.title: 1. Install WSL
docs.text:
Open PowerShell as Administrator:

  1. Open the Start menu.
  2. Search for PowerShell.
  3. Right-click Windows PowerShell and select Run as administrator.

Run:

wsl --install

This installs WSL 2 and Ubuntu by default.

Restart Windows when prompted.

docs.title: 2. Create your Linux account
docs.text:
After restarting, open Ubuntu from the Start menu.

The first launch completes the installation and asks you to create:

Enter new UNIX username:
New password:
Retype new password:

Choose a username and password.

When entering a Linux password, nothing appears on screen. This is normal.

This account is separate from your Windows account and can perform administrative tasks using sudo.

docs.title: 3. Update Ubuntu
docs.text:
Once the Linux terminal opens, run:

sudo apt update
sudo apt upgrade -y

Enter the Linux password you created when prompted.

docs.title: 4. Check the installation
docs.text:
From PowerShell, run:

wsl --list --verbose

You should see something similar to:

NAME      STATE     VERSION
Ubuntu    Running   2

The VERSION should normally be 2.

docs.title: 5. Start WSL
docs.text:
You can start Ubuntu from the Start menu or directly from PowerShell:

wsl

To leave Linux:

exit

You now have a working Linux environment inside Windows able to connect to Hyperion without issues

docs.title: Installing Mamba
docs.text:
Mamba is a fast package and environment manager compatible with Conda.

On the cluster, install it in your personal storage directory:

/storage/<your-username>/

Do not install it into the system directories.

docs.title: 1. Go to your storage directory
docs.text:
cd /storage/<your-username>

You can usually replace <your-username> with $USER:

cd /storage/$USER

docs.title: 2. Download Miniforge
docs.text:
Miniforge includes both Conda and Mamba.

wget -O Miniforge3.sh \
  "https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge/releases/latest/download/Miniforge3-$(uname)-$(uname -m).sh"

docs.title: 3. Install it
docs.text:
Install Miniforge into your storage directory:

bash Miniforge3.sh -b -p /storage/$USER/miniforge3

The -b option performs the installation without interactive prompts.

You can now remove the installer:

rm Miniforge3.sh

docs.title: 4. Enable Mamba
docs.text:
Load Conda and Mamba:

source /storage/$USER/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh
source /storage/$USER/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/mamba.sh

To make them available automatically whenever you log in, add these lines to ~/.bashrc:

echo 'source /storage/$USER/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh' >> ~/.bashrc
echo 'source /storage/$USER/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/mamba.sh' >> ~/.bashrc

Reload your shell:

source ~/.bashrc

Check that Mamba works:

mamba --version

docs.title: Linux Command Line Cheat Sheet
docs.text: A short reference for navigating and managing files from a Linux terminal.

docs.title: Paths and directories
docs.text:
Linux uses / to separate folders.

/home/username/projects/data

Useful path shortcuts:

Symbol Meaning / Root of the filesystem ~ Your home directory . Current directory .. Parent directory

An absolute path starts from /:

cd /home/username/projects

A relative path starts from your current directory:

cd projects/data

docs.title: Where am I?
docs.text:
Print your current directory:

pwd

Example:

/home/username/projects

docs.title: List files and folders
docs.text:
ls

Useful options:

ls -l      # detailed list
ls -a      # include hidden files
ls -lh     # detailed list with human-readable file sizes
ls -lah    # combine the above

List another directory without moving into it:

ls /path/to/directory

docs.title: Move between directories
docs.text:
Enter a directory:

cd projects

Move up one level:

cd ..

Return to your home directory:

cd ~

or simply:

cd

Move using an absolute path:

cd /home/username/projects

Tip: Press Tab to autocomplete file and directory names.

docs.title: Create files and directories
docs.text:
Create a directory:

mkdir results

Create nested directories:

mkdir -p project/data/raw

Create an empty file:

touch notes.txt

docs.title: Copy files and directories
docs.text:
Copy a file:

cp file.txt file_copy.txt

Copy a file into another directory:

cp file.txt results/

Copy a directory and everything inside it:

cp -r data data_backup

docs.title: Move and rename files
docs.text:
Move a file:

mv file.txt results/

Rename a file:

mv old_name.txt new_name.txt

The same command works for directories:

mv old_folder new_folder

docs.title: Delete files and directories
docs.text:
Delete a file:

rm file.txt

Delete an empty directory:

rmdir folder

Delete a directory and its contents:

rm -r folder

Be careful with:

rm -rf folder

rm permanently deletes files. There is normally no recycle bin on a Linux server.

docs.title: View file contents
docs.text:
Print a small file:

cat file.txt

Read a longer file interactively:

less file.txt

Useful keys inside less:

↑ / ↓    move
Space    next page
q        quit

Show the first lines of a file:

head file.txt

Show the last lines:

tail file.txt

Follow a file as new lines are added, useful for log files:

tail -f job.log

Press Ctrl+C to stop following it.

docs.title: Edit files with Nano
docs.text:
Open or create a file:

nano script.sh

Nano displays its shortcuts at the bottom of the screen. ^ means Ctrl.

Important shortcuts:

Shortcut Action Ctrl+O Save Ctrl+X Exit Ctrl+W Search Ctrl+K Cut line Ctrl+U Paste

To save and exit:

  1. Press Ctrl+O
  2. Press Enter to confirm the filename
  3. Press Ctrl+X

docs.title: Find files
docs.text:
Find a file below the current directory:

find . -name "results.csv"

Find all Python files:

find . -name "*.py"

Search somewhere else:

find /path/to/search -name "*.csv"

docs.title: Search inside files
docs.text:
Search for text in a file:

grep "error" job.log

Ignore capitalization:

grep -i "error" job.log

Search recursively through a directory:

grep -r "species_id" scripts/

docs.title: Useful terminal shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut / command Action Tab Autocomplete ↑ / ↓ Browse command history Ctrl+C Stop the current command Ctrl+L Clear the screen clear Clear the screen history Show previous commands

docs.title: File permissions
docs.text:
If you see:

Permission denied

check the file permissions:

ls -l

Permissions are shown as:

-rwxr-xr--

where:

  • r = read
  • w = write
  • x = execute

Make a script executable:

chmod +x script.sh

Then run it with:

./script.sh

On shared clusters, do not change permissions unless you understand who should have access to the files.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text:
pwd                     # show current directory
ls -lah                 # list files
cd folder               # enter folder
cd ..                   # move up
cd ~                    # go home
mkdir folder            # create directory
touch file.txt          # create empty file
cp file.txt copy.txt    # copy file
cp -r dir copy          # copy directory
mv old.txt new.txt      # move or rename
rm file.txt             # delete file
rm -r folder            # delete directory
cat file.txt            # print file
less file.txt           # inspect file
nano file.txt           # edit file
find . -name "*.csv"    # find files
grep "text" file.txt    # search inside file

docs.title: Using Mamba
docs.text: Mamba manages isolated software environments. On a cluster, use a separate environment for each project rather than installing packages into base.

docs.title: Create an environment
docs.text:
Create an empty environment:

mamba create -n myproject

Create an environment with R:

mamba create -n myproject r-base

Or install a specific R version:

mamba create -n myproject r-base=4.4

To see which R versions are available:

mamba search r-base

You can install several packages when creating the environment:

mamba create -n myproject r-base=4.4 r-tidyverse r-sf

Packages are installed from the configured Conda channels. With Miniforge, conda-forge is normally the default.

docs.title: Activate and deactivate environments
docs.text:
Activate an environment:

mamba activate myproject

Your prompt will usually change to show the active environment:

(myproject) username@cluster:~$

Deactivate it:

mamba deactivate

List your environments:

mamba env list

docs.title: Install packages
docs.text:
Activate the environment first:

mamba activate myproject

Then install packages:

mamba install r-data.table

Install several packages at once:

mamba install r-tidyverse r-sf r-terra

Most R packages on conda-forge use the prefix r-:

R package Mamba package tidyverse r-tidyverse sf r-sf terra r-terra data.table r-data.table

Search for a package:

mamba search r-raster

You can also install Python packages in the same way:

mamba install python=3.12 numpy pandas

docs.title: Install packages from inside R
docs.text:
If a package is not available through Mamba, activate the environment and start R:

mamba activate myproject
R

Then install it normally:

install.packages("package_name")

Prefer Mamba packages when available, especially for packages with compiled system dependencies such as sf, terra, or raster.

docs.title: Update packages
docs.text:
Update a specific package:

mamba update r-sf

Update all packages in the active environment:

mamba update --all

docs.title: Remove packages or environments
docs.text:
Remove a package:

mamba remove r-sf

Remove an entire environment:

mamba env remove -n myproject

docs.title: Save an environment
docs.text:
Export the environment to a YAML file:

mamba env export > environment.yml

Recreate it later with:

mamba env create -f environment.yml

A simple environment.yml can also be written manually:

name: myproject

channels:
  - conda-forge

dependencies:
  - r-base=4.4
  - r-tidyverse
  - r-sf
  - r-terra

Then create the environment with:

mamba env create -f environment.yml

docs.title: Typical workflow
docs.text:
# Create the environment once
mamba create -n myproject r-base=4.4 r-tidyverse r-sf

# Activate it whenever you work on the project
mamba activate myproject

# Run R
R

# Leave the environment when finished
mamba deactivate
